caption: Dashboard on first load: six seeded tasks-as-processes in the READY state, idle resource bars, and an empty AI SYSTEM feed.
Processes screen: every task is a process with a PID, priority, burst time, memory/CPU requirement, and an enforced lifecycle state.
Creating a new task through the form: name, description, priority, burst time (minutes), memory (MB) and CPU (%) requirements.
The new task is admitted as PID 7 and moves NEW to READY automatically, persisted to SQLite.

Scheduler: FCFS. First-Come-First-Served: tasks run strictly in arrival order. Simple and full-utilisation, but long tasks can delay everything behind them (the convoy effect). The page shows the Gantt chart, per-process timing metrics, and Jain's Fairness Index.

Scheduler: SJF. Shortest-Job-First: the shortest tasks are dispatched first, minimising average wait for short work at the risk of starving long tasks. The page shows the Gantt chart, per-process timing metrics, and Jain's Fairness Index.

Scheduler: Priority. Priority scheduling using Procura's effective-priority score (user priority + deadline urgency + waiting-time aging + resource cost + Slurm-style fair-share decay). The page shows the Gantt chart, per-process timing metrics, and Jain's Fairness Index.

Scheduler: Round Robin. Round Robin with a fixed quantum: every task gets a turn in rotation, bounding the worst-case wait between turns. The page shows the Gantt chart, per-process timing metrics, and Jain's Fairness Index.

Scheduler: EEVDF. EEVDF, Linux's default scheduler since kernel 6.6: dispatches the eligible task with the earliest virtual deadline, approximating an ideal fair share. The page shows the Gantt chart, per-process timing metrics, and Jain's Fairness Index.

Scheduler: MLFQ. Multi-Level Feedback Queue (OSTEP's five rules): tasks are demoted after exhausting their allotment and periodically boosted back to the top queue to prevent starvation. The page shows the Gantt chart, per-process timing metrics, and Jain's Fairness Index.
Dashboard under resource contention: the low-priority 'Weekly grocery run' (P3) is hogging 1200 MB and P1 holds 600 MB, leaving only 248 MB of the 2048 MB simulated memory pool for everything else.
Error Monitor before detection: no errors logged yet, with the RUN DETECT NOW control available.

Error Monitor after one detection pass, showing all three recovery outcomes: suspend_and_retry (a strictly lower-priority holder is preempted because doing so frees enough memory), retry (memory freed by an earlier recovery is reused), and memory_failure_no_victim (no lower-priority holder could free enough, so the task is left pending rather than evicting higher-priority work for nothing).
An expanded diagnosis: the AI explanation is grounded in the recorded incident facts (requested vs. available memory) and the retrieved Memory_Management / Error_Recovery knowledge-base passages.
Dashboard after automatic recovery: the AI SYSTEM feed shows each detect, diagnose and recover event, and memory utilisation reflects the preempted low-priority task and the retried allocations.
AI Assistant grounded on a specific process (P5): the answer combines retrieved knowledge-base passages with the live process state.
AI Assistant answering a general OS-concepts question, retrieved from the six-document knowledge base.
Auto-generated interactive API documentation (FastAPI /docs) listing all 16 REST endpoints.

procura_top, the htop-style terminal dashboard: the same live process table, resource utilisation bars and AI SYSTEM feed as the web dashboard, rendered with the rich library and polling the same REST API.

The benchmark module running all six algorithms against an identical, seeded 30-job Poisson workload and printing the standard metric set (makespan, turnaround, waiting time, utilisation, Jain's Fairness Index, max wait, starvation count).
The automated test suite: every scheduling algorithm, state transition, resource-contention path, statistical detector and recovery script is verified, with all tests passing.
